note: GROUND TRUTH for the yacht domain. The sim reads this to build the scalar fields and to score detections. No sensor, detector or agent may import it — the same boundary as the house's, and the same test.
_theFinding: Three faults are missed, and the three misses have three different reasons, which is the point. yc-04 is the most severe fault on the vessel and it is a condensation in the forward stringer void, whose only apertures are two 200 mm deck hatches; the ground bot is 340 mm across, the hover bot needs 400 mm of clearance, and the inchworm is confined to conduits. The nearest candidate the swarm raised was 6.41 m away. That one is ARCHITECTURE: the boat stopped the swarm. yc-07 is also architectural in effect - the deckhead void is 410 mm and the hover bot faulted on an empty battery - and yc-02 is a DETECTION miss, because the blocked-vent detector's gate sits above the whole range of the air field. The report says which is which rather than dressing them all up as coverage.
_onTaxonomy: `class` is the marine CAUSE — what a surveyor would write on the report. `signature` is the physical READING the detector produces, in the generic vocabulary. They are different things and are kept in different fields because five marine causes share the `moisture_leak` reading and the instrument cannot tell them apart: yc-03, yc-04 and yc-07 are an active leak, a condensation and a hygroscopic salt equilibrium, and they look identical to a humidity sensor. The instrument finds a reading; the taxonomy says what the reading is consistent with; the distinction is the product's honesty and the reason the report never names a cause it cannot support.
_onMissReason: A per-fault reason for a miss, in the same spirit as the house's `crackLimitation` note: a fault that is reported as missed carries the structural reason with it, rather than being presented as a bare 0.00. A miss with a reason is a finding. A miss without one is a defect.

anomalies.note: A weeping exhaust joint in the engine bay. The thermal signature is the tell: the exhaust runs hot and the leak runs cold against it. The instrument cannot name the gasket — that is the yard's call — but it can put a mark on the manifold and say the temperature there is not what the rest of the manifold is doing.

anomalies.missReason: DETECTION, not coverage. The nearest candidate is 0.63 m away, so the swarm was at the vent. The blocked-vent detector did not fire because the air proxy at the port rose 118% over the field's ambient and the detector's gate is a 150% rise - the entire field peaks below the threshold, so no position in the engine bay would have triggered it. That is a calibration finding and not a boat finding, and it is the kind of thing this twin exists to surface: the house's gate does not transfer to a boat. The crawler's obstruction finding cannot be credited to this fault either, and the manifold is why - that reading is from inside the fuel line, and an obstruction in a 60 mm bore is not a blocked air path in the room.
anomalies.note: The engine bay extraction inlet is obstructed. Stale air accumulates and everything in the bay runs warmer, which is what makes every other thermal reading in this compartment harder to interpret.

An active leak in the engine bay. The swarm finds the reading and the report says 'a moisture anomaly of undetermined cause' — because a condensation and a historic salt would read the same. What the owner does with that is the deployment: wash the deck, watch whether it comes back.

anomalies.missReason: UNREACHABLE, and it is the most severe fault on the vessel. The forward stringer void is entered only through two 200 mm deck hatches. The ground bot is 340 mm across, the hover bot is 240 mm across, and the inchworm is confined to conduits, of which the void has none. A person cannot get their body through a 200 mm hand-hole either - but a person can kneel on the deck, put an arm and a torch through it, and reach this fault 760 mm below. Nothing in the swarm can get within 340 mm of the hole. The nearest candidate the swarm raised was 6.41 m away, in the engine room, and its sensor range is 3 m.
anomalies.note: The fault the whole product exists for, and it sits directly under the forward deck hatch: 760 mm below the deck, inside a space that is entered from nowhere else. Condensation in a void is the most common void fault on any boat and the one nobody reports, because it needs somebody to have put an arm in there. That is still a person-and-a-torch job today. A person's arm reaches it; nothing in the swarm can get its sensor within 340 mm of the hole.

A drain run obstructed by stowage sitting over the grating, and the obstruction is physically in the content file, so the swarm has something to find. Note what the instrument contributes: an obstruction, at a place on the map. It cannot tell a blocked drain from a stowed toolbox, and the report does not pretend otherwise - it is the same reading either way.

Debris in the fuel supply line, found by the crawler looking down the bore. A 60 mm fuel line is a good place to put a robot and a bad place to put a person, and it is the clearest case in the taxonomy for the swarm earning its keep.

anomalies.missReason: TOO TALL, and on the wrong manifold. The deckhead void over the engine is 410 mm and the hover bot's clearance is 1.0 m: it went in, spent its entire 12 Wh pack holding station against the ceiling, and faulted on empty without a candidate. The ground bot's humidity reading does reach the source - the nearest candidate is 0.73 m away - but it is a reading taken on the sole, 850 mm below the fault, and a reading on the ground manifold cannot be credited to a fault in the deckhead void. Two reasons, one of them costing the whole battery.
anomalies.note: Salt in the core, in equilibrium with the boat's own ambient. Even if the swarm had got there, the honest answer would have been 'consistent with hygroscopic salt, not provable without a sample' — the one class in the taxonomy where the instrument says less than the owner wants to hear, and is right.
